explain.say: Each stripe pattern is a unit called a sarcomere, made of two kinds of thin threads: actin and myosin. They overlap like fingers of two hands slotted together.

explain.say: When a nerve signal arrives, myosin heads grab the actin, pull, let go and grab again, using energy from ATP. The threads slide past each other, every sarcomere shortens, and the whole muscle contracts.

faq.a: They are protein filaments inside muscle fibres. Thick myosin filaments have little heads that grab thin actin filaments and pull them along, making the muscle shorten.
asks: Tell me about actin and myosin

faq.a: A muscle fibre is a single, very long muscle cell, sometimes many centimetres long, with many nuclei. Thousands of fibres bundled together make a muscle.
asks: Tell me about the muscle fibre

faq.a: A nerve signal reaches the muscle fibre and releases calcium inside it. Calcium uncovers grabbing sites on actin so the myosin heads can attach and pull.
asks: How does a nerve make a muscle move?

faq.a: Contraction works by filaments sliding together to shorten the muscle. Nothing in the fibre can push the filaments apart, so a muscle relaxes and is stretched back by another muscle.
Skeletal muscle has regular repeating sarcomeres. The overlapping actin and myosin make light and dark bands, so it looks striped, or striated, under a microscope.

facts: The sliding filament theory was proposed in 1954 by two independent teams, including Andrew Huxley and Hugh Huxley.
Myosin uses energy from ATP to pull on actin filaments.

quiz.say: What happens to actin and myosin when a muscle contracts?
quiz.show: What happens to actin and myosin when a muscle contracts?
quiz.why: The filaments keep their length; they slide further over each other so each sarcomere shortens.

wrong.0: The filaments do not shrink; their overlap increases.
wrong.2: They grab and release repeatedly; they do not fuse.
